correctness.rationale: In a p-periodic interval of length at least 2p every marker has a partner at distance p. Therefore the only possible nonconstant run with b>0 has p=b+1, and there is at most one after maximal extension. It extends min(a,b) to the left and min(c,b) to the right: any further step, if present, would force a third marker. Least period follows by the same partner test at every smaller period. The length threshold is exactly a+c≥b. The period-one terms are the zero blocks of length at least two and the adjacent ones if b=0. Thus all four terms first occur at (2,2,2), and extending an outer gap preserves them; direct gap budget at smaller n gives the stated maxima. For the bivariate identity, for m=a+c the extra term has middle-gap weight 1 for b=0, z for b=1 if m≥1, and u times the finite geometric sum z² through z^m for b≥2 if m≥2; this yields the displayed bracket. Translating all gaps by two gives t=n−8, with admissible middle gap B≤(t+2)/2. The excluded triples have B=A+C+3+e with e≥0, giving exactly the subtracted rational term. Summing over B gives the stated closed form and its 3/4 fraction limit. A separate maximal equality-stretch computation tested 2,600 words of lengths 2 to 25 and matched the counts and higher-period intervals; for n=8,9,10,11,12 the four-run counts are 1,3,6,9,14.
residual_risks: Finite enumeration corroborates the classification; the formal-series and all-length assertions follow from the proof, not from interpolation of finite data.

evidence: The distinct-alphabet parameter d=2 bounds arbitrary binary words and does not encode fixed composition; at n=8 its bound is 5, not 4. Fischer et al.'s 22n/23 bound is likewise not exact for this slice.

The later three-marker catalogue listing studies a different slice. The later two-marker exponent proof, although its target is a different statistic, explicitly exhausts all runs and obtains length b+2+min(a,b)+min(c,b) for the sole possible higher-period interval.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Inspect the ingredients of the closer theorem, not just its output statistic: its later proof gives exact underlying coverage; the general worst-case bounds do not.

evidence: The same-day square proof gives max(0,b−c)≤u≤min(a,b). This interval is nonempty exactly when a+c≥b. Its extremal splits give left extent min(a,b) and right extent b−max(0,b−c)=min(c,b). Each marked square for b>0 is primitive in the required least-period sense because a shorter period would pair a marker at smaller displacement. Every nonconstant run contains such a marked square, and the resultant union is maximal at that period. Period-one runs are immediate from the three gaps and b=0.

The later exponent proof states the same eligibility test L≥2(b+1) and extensions; the submitted generating function then uses only summation over the allowed middle-gap interval with one extra u weight.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The different statistic in the same-day title does not prevent coverage of the central statement. The distribution is an additional evaluation, not an earlier published formula established by this comparison.

evidence: Bannai et al. use the same maximal least-period definition. Madden counts maximal constant blocks only.

For exactly two ones, a square containing both markers occurs uniquely at the position determined by its ordered split (u,v), with u+v=b. Its legal u values form a single interval; the extension to the maximal run contains exactly the union of the marked square intervals for b>0.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Constant-block runs are not equivalent, but here the marked square classification is position-complete and can be converted to the unique marked maximal-period interval.

originality.rationale: The distinct same-day exact-square record does not count runs, but its full position-determining classification of marked squares already gives the central run classification by maximal extension, with no further combinatorial case analysis. The later exponent record explicitly proves precisely the same least-period-one and higher-period run classification. Neither source is credited with stating the frozen bivariate formula; its geometric-sum enumeration is correct but is a direct reweighting of the covered interval classification, not enough to support the combined frozen finding as a distinct contribution. Calendar dates do not resolve within-day order or establish that the later exponent record has priority.
residual_risks: No within-day priority determined. The later exponent result is evidence of overlap, not evidence of priority.
